On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge posted a computer-checkable proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the most
famous open problems in mathematics. I'm checking it myself, from scratch, on my own hardware. This page follows that
check live: it updates as each step finishes, and every result on it is quoted from the run's logs.

{{< include _status.md >}}

## What Is the Riemann Hypothesis?

Prime numbers (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …) are the building blocks of whole numbers: every whole number is a product
of primes in exactly one way. They get rarer as numbers grow, but they never follow a simple pattern. Look at any
stretch of numbers and the primes seem scattered almost at random.

In the 1790s, Gauss noticed that the *number* of primes up to any point follows a smooth curve surprisingly well.
In 1859, Bernhard Riemann found a way to describe exactly how far the true count wanders from that curve. The
errors are controlled by the zeros of a function now called the Riemann zeta function, written ζ(s). His
hypothesis is that all of those zeros (apart from some easy ones at −2, −4, −6, …) sit on a single straight line,
where the real part of *s* is ½. If that's true, the primes are as evenly spread as they could possibly be. Their
irregularity is like the static of a coin-flip sequence, never anything worse.

Why it matters:

- **It's the most famous open problem in mathematics.** It was on Hilbert's 1900 list of the century's key
  problems, and it is one of the Clay Institute's seven
  [Millennium Prize Problems](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/riemann-hypothesis/), with a \$1 million prize.
- **A lot of mathematics is built on it.** Thousands of published results begin "assuming the Riemann
  Hypothesis…". A proof would turn every one of them into a theorem.
- **It has resisted the best mathematicians for 167 years,** despite checks of the first trillions of zeros, which
  all lie on the line.

(It wouldn't break internet encryption, a common worry. That depends on how hard it is to factor large numbers,
which this doesn't change.)

## What Happened

On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge posted a [short remark](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf) and a 1.4 GB project
written in [Lean](https://lean-lang.org), claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, along with the same statement
for every Dirichlet L-function (a whole family of close relatives of ζ). The proof was written with AI, and it is
enormous: 175,187 files and about 17 million lines.

No person can read a proof that size. Lean is what makes it checkable anyway. Lean is a proof assistant: a program
whose small core, the *kernel*, accepts a proof only if every single step follows from the rules of logic. That
turns "is this proof right?" into a question anyone with a powerful enough computer can answer, as long as they're
careful about exactly what they check.

Within hours, people in the Lean community had built it and run it through several independent checkers (see the
[forum thread](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/113488-general/topic/Discussion.3A.20Alp.C3.B6ge.20Proves.20the.20Riemann.20Hypothesis)).
The most complete public record is [Andrew Sutherland's page](https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/), which this page is
modelled on.

## Why I'm Checking It Myself

I wanted to do it end to end, for my own understanding, and to feel a small part of history being made.

I also have mixed feelings about it, and a lot of uncertainty about how AI will shape the future. Only weeks ago,
in a [Numberphile interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bAnwMdfcMVw), I remember Terence Tao saying he
didn't expect the Riemann Hypothesis to be solved until around 2050. Now there is a claimed proof, written with AI,
that Lean's checkers accept. The only thing anyone can say with certainty is that nothing is off the table.

## What a Check Can and Can't Tell You

If every check passes, it means Lean's kernel, and several independent checkers, accepted a proof of five exact
formal statements, using nothing beyond Lean's three standard axioms. It does **not** mean:

- **that anyone understands the proof.** Understanding it is the work of mathematicians, and it will take years;
- **that the formal statements mean what we think.** That is why they are spelled out in the next section;
- **that the checkers can't all share one bug.** They were written independently, in different languages, and
  some come with formal proofs of their own correctness, which makes a shared bug very unlikely.

## The Five Statements

A proof is only as good as the statement it proves, so the check starts by pinning down exactly what has to be
proved. It does that with two separate files.

- **The challenge** is a short file that only *states* the five theorems. It doesn't prove anything. Lean won't
  accept a theorem without a proof attached, so each one ends in `sorry`, Lean's placeholder for a proof left blank.
- **The solution** is the project's own `Main.lean`. It states theorems with the same five names and supplies the
  real proofs.

A checker then compares the two: the statements must mean exactly the same thing, and the proofs must be complete
and accepted by the kernel.

**Why a separate file?** Building the project runs code the project contains, and that code can change what
words mean inside it. Kevin Buzzard demonstrates this in talks by redefining exponentiation so that something that
*looks* like Fermat's Last Theorem becomes trivially "provable". In the forum thread about this proof, someone
showed that one line of `notation` can make `RiemannHypothesis` mean `True`. Reading the project's own copy of the
statements would not catch that. The challenge imports nothing but Mathlib, Lean's shared math library, whose
definition of the Riemann Hypothesis was written long before this project existed. It is built before any project
code runs, so nothing in the project can tamper with it.

The five statements, in words:

| Theorem | In Words |
|---|---|
| `riemannHypothesis` | Mathlib's `RiemannHypothesis`: every zero of ζ other than −2, −4, −6, … (and the pole at 1) has real part ½. |
| `riemannZeta_eq_zero_re` | The same statement, written out. |
| `LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re` | For every modulus N and Dirichlet character χ, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 when Re s > ½, except at the pole χ = 1, s = 1. |
| `LFunction_eq_zero_re` | Every zero of every Dirichlet L-function in the strip 0 < Re s < 1 has Re s = ½. |
| `LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive` | The same, for primitive characters. |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The challenge file in Lean"}
```lean
import Mathlib

def RiemannZetaZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

def DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

def DirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ),
    0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

def PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine : Prop :=
  ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive →
    ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis := by sorry
theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : RiemannZetaZerosOnLine := by sorry
theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : DirichletLNonvanishingRightOfHalf := by sorry
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : DirichletLZerosOnLine := by sorry
theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : PrimitiveDirichletLZerosOnLine := by sorry
```
:::

I'm not a number theorist, so I don't rely on my own reading of the last four. They have to match the project's
definitions term for term, which the checkers enforce, and they agree with the version reviewed in public by people
who are.

**Where this comes from.** The challenge-and-solution setup isn't mine. It is the Lean FRO's
[Comparator](https://github.com/leanprover/comparator) model, which the community applied to this project in
[Deicyde/riemann-hypothesis](https://github.com/Deicyde/riemann-hypothesis); Kevin Buzzard's
[post](https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/) explains why each part
matters. I wrote my challenge file independently, and apart from comments it is identical to the community's
[`Challenge.lean`](https://github.com/Deicyde/riemann-hypothesis/blob/main/src/Challenge.lean). It has to be: the
statements are fixed by the project, and the checker requires them to match exactly. When I build their file with
my Mathlib, it comes out byte for byte the same as theirs.

**What this check adds.** The challenge file only fixes *what* is checked. Everything around it is where this run
goes further than the basic setup:

- **Sandboxed build in a fresh VM.** The project is compiled with the network off, inside a Landlock sandbox
  that was tested before use, so the code that builds the proof can't touch anything else.
- **Mathlib from source.** Mathlib is compiled from source and compared file by file with its official build cache,
  so the check doesn't rely on prebuilt files.
- **Nine checkers.** Beyond Comparator's Lean kernel and nanoda, the proof also goes to con-leche (including its
  `--compare` mode, a formally verified second implementation of the statement comparison), con-ron, lean4lean,
  Pestka and nanoclo.
- **Secondary checks.** An axiom audit that walks every constant itself, a per-module kernel replay, and checks that
  no source file or tool changed during the run.
- **Hashes against other runs.** My build and export are compared with the hashes other people published, so a
  match shows we checked the same bytes.

The formal proof itself doesn't claim more than these five statements. Alpöge's remark says the method should
extend further, but the Lean project proves exactly these five, and those are what get checked.

### Checkers

Each checker reads the same exported proof and either accepts it, rejects it, or fails to finish. A rejection by
any one of them would override every acceptance.

{{< include _kernels.md >}}

### Hashes You Can Compare

A hash is a fingerprint of a file: change one byte and it changes completely. Matching hashes mean my run checked
the same proof as other public runs, and that the build reproduces bit for bit on a different machine, built a
different way (sandboxed here, unsandboxed elsewhere).

{{< include _hashes.md >}}

## What Happens Next

The project build takes roughly a day on this machine. After it come the export, then the checkers; the slowest,
Lean's own kernel replaying the full 61 GB proof on a single thread, may take another day or more. This page updates
as each one reports. When the last result is in, I'll write up what I found here, whatever it is.

## How I Used AI

It felt right to check an AI-written proof with an AI's help, and also strange. Claude (Anthropic's AI) set up and
ran this check with me: it wrote the scripts, ran the commands and drafted this page, and I reviewed and directed
the work. That is exactly why the check is built so that no single party has to be trusted, including the AI
running it. Every result here is read from logs, and the hashes let anyone confirm that the same bytes were checked.
It doesn't settle my mixed feelings about AI, but it does show one thing it can't take away: a proof that anyone
can check for themselves.

## Technical Notes

### How the Check Works

I treated the project as untrusted code. Building a Lean project runs code it contains (tactics, macros, build
commands), so nothing from it ran on my own machine, and nothing that loads it ran outside a sandbox.

1. **A fresh virtual machine** with its own kernel. Every tool is pinned to an exact commit and verified, and the
   project is downloaded and checked inside the VM.
2. **No network** once the downloads are done. Mathlib is then compiled from source and compared file by file with
   Mathlib's official build cache.
3. **The statements first.** The challenge file is built and exported before any project code runs.
4. **A sandbox for the project.** The build runs under [Landlock](https://landlock.io) via
   [landrun](https://github.com/Zouuup/landrun): it can read its sources and the toolchain and write only its own
   build folder. Before starting, I tested that writes elsewhere, reading SSH keys and network connections all fail.
5. **Export, then judge.** The compiled proof is exported to a single file, and the judges read only that file, so
   no project code runs while checking. `lake comparator` checks that the statements match the challenge and that
   only `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice` are used, then replays the whole proof through Lean's kernel.
   Then the proof goes through every independent checker that fits in the VM's memory.

### Findings along the Way

::: {.callout-note title="Mathlib from Source Matches the Official Cache, with One Exception"}
Of the 8,700 files in Mathlib's official build cache, 8,689 are byte-identical to my from-source build. Ten belong
to the cache tool itself and aren't part of the math. One differs:
`Mathlib/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/Walk/Operations.olean`, and only in a single auto-generated lemma,
`SimpleGraph.Walk.take.eq_2`. The other 230 constants in that file match. My build of it is deterministic (rebuilt
twice, same bytes), so the cache's copy was produced differently. Both versions are kernel-checked theorems; this is
a reproducibility quirk, not a soundness problem.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="A Full Build Needs about 1.7 TB of Bookkeeping"}
For each module, Lake writes a `.setup.json` file listing everything it imports. Here that averages about 7 MB, and
a sampled estimate over all 175,187 modules is about 1.7 TB. The files compress about 26× with zstd, so this run
builds on a compressed btrfs disk.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Two Problems the Tests Caught"}
My sandbox wrapper first failed in a way that looked like success: the kernel supports Landlock ABI v6, landrun
asked for v10 and refused to start, and every "access denied" test passed because nothing ran at all. A positive
control (a command that must succeed) now runs first. Separately, the original checker script counted `sorry`
warnings with the wrong quote characters, so that count could never be non-zero; it's
[fixed](https://github.com/kai-do/riemann-hypothesis-lean-check). The axiom check was never affected.
:::
